study_identification_part.si4_title: A normative modelling approach reveals age-atypical cortical thickness in a subgroup of males with autism spectrum disorder

study_characteristics_part.sc1_study_objective: To examine how cortical thickness (CT) in Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) can be parameterized as an individualized metric of atypicality relative to typically-developing (TD) age-related norms, and to isolate subgroups with highly age-atypical CT.

caa6_deviation_metric.answer: w-score (analogous to a z-score), calculated for each brain region for each individual. A cutoff of |w| > 2 was used to define 'significant' atypicality.
caa6_deviation_metric.reason: The paper defines the w-score and its calculation, and specifies the threshold used to identify outliers.
caa6_deviation_metric.supporting_text: These statistical norms were then used to compute a w-score (analogous to a z -score) for every individual with autism and every brain region... We operationalized ' signi /uniFB01 cant ' atypicality in statistical terms as w-scores >2 SD away from TD norms.

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa7_association_analysis: Spearman correlations for each brain region between w-scores and phenotypic features (ADOS, SRS, SCQ, AQ, FIQ and Age), with FDR correction for multiple comparisons.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa8_key_findings_brief: A small subgroup of males with ASD shows highly age-atypical cortical thickness, and these individuals drive the small on-average case-control differences often reported; this normative approach also reveals brain-behavior associations not seen with traditional methods.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa9_key_findings_detailed: Conventional case-control analyses identified small cortical thickness (CT) differences in 8.7% of brain regions, but these effects were halved by removing a small subgroup of 'outlier' patients with highly atypical CT (w-scores > 2 SD). This subgroup had a median prevalence of 7.6% across brain regions. An analysis of the w-scores themselves revealed a different set of regions showing on-average atypicality. Furthermore, these individualized w-scores correlated with symptom severity (ADOS and SRS scores) in frontal, parietal, and temporal regions, areas largely distinct from those identified in case-control analyses.

caa10_key_limitations.answer: 1. Cross-sectional data limits claims about individual developmental trajectories. 2. Heterogeneity of the ABIDE dataset (scanners, acquisition parameters). 3. The LOESS modeling approach may be less reliable in age-bins with sparse data. 4. The analysis was restricted to males, limiting generalizability to females.
caa10_key_limitations.supporting_text: First and foremost, the present data are cross-sectional and the normative age modelling approach cannot make claims about trajectories at an individual level. ... Second, the dataset also presents a post-hoc collection of sites accumulated through the ABIDE initiative, whereby scanners, imaging acquisition sequences and parameters, sample ascertainment, etc., are highly heterogeneous. ... Third, there are a number of different approaches to normative modelling that all have pros and cons... Hence in situations where data is spare the LOESS approach may allow for less reliable normative scores. ... we conducted normative modelling on the male group only

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa11_application_notes: The study introduces a method to identify 'statistical outlier' patients based on normative models and demonstrates that removing these individuals significantly alters the results of traditional case-control analyses. It also calculates a 'global w-score ratio' to distinguish between region-specific and globally atypical individuals.

general_note_part.gn1_general_notes: The study also performed the same normative modeling analysis on cortical volume, surface area, and local gyrification index (LGI), with similar findings that small case-control differences are largely driven by outlier individuals (see Supplementary Figures S9-S12).
